page: Microsoft Azure E4-2ads_v7 is an x86_64 architecture server powered by a dedicated AMD EPYC 9V45 processor running at 4.5 GHz. It features 1 physical core with 2 threads, representing 2 vCPUs, and is configured with 32.0 GB of system memory, yielding a high memory-to-core ratio of 16.0 GB per core. The server includes 236 GB of local storage, is Premium Storage capable, and runs on the Microsoft Hyper-V hypervisor.

Benchmark data reveals a significant divergence between single-core and multi-core capabilities. Single-core performance is highly competitive, with stress-ng single-core CPU performance, single-threaded gzip compression, and single-threaded bzip3 decompression all placing in the top 10% tier. Conversely, due to the low physical core count, multi-core CPU performance and Passmark CPU scores fall into the bottom 25% tier. Large-block memory bandwidth read and write speeds remain in the middle 50% tier, while small-block cached read bandwidth is in the bottom 25%.

The server exhibits weak performance in multi-threaded workloads, database operations, and static web serving, all scoring in the bottom 25% tier. However, its high memory density relative to CPU resources makes it qualitatively cost-efficient for memory-bound workloads that do not require high parallel processing power. It is suited for single-threaded data processing, lightweight memory-intensive caching, and small-scale LLM inference tasks using smaller models.

Equipped with 32.0 GB of RAM and 236 GB of local storage, this server provides a high memory-to-vCPU ratio. In benchmark testing, it demonstrates top-tier single-core CPU performance, single-threaded gzip compression, and single-threaded bzip3 decompression. However, its multi-core CPU performance, database operations, and static web serving throughput fall into the bottom 25% tier due to the single physical core constraint. This hardware profile is qualitatively cost-efficient for memory-intensive, single-threaded workloads, lightweight caching, and small-scale model inference, rather than highly parallelized or database-heavy applications.
